meta.title: Hybrid Diagnostic Booking — Ayushi Maurya
meta.description: Redesigning a health app's diagnostic booking so users can book pathology and radiology tests together in one booking, with pathology at home or at a centre.

content.title: One booking for a complete full-body checkup
content.dek: In most health apps, a "full body checkup" means blood tests with home sample collection, and nothing else. I redesigned the diagnostic booking flow so a full-body checkup includes radiology too. Users can book pathology and radiology in one booking, with pathology at home or at a centre.

media.alt: The redesigned lab tests home and booking flow

content.label: 01 The problem
content.heading: Most "full body checkups" left out radiology
paragraphs: Most health apps sell "full body checkup" packages that only include pathology tests with home sample collection. A complete checkup also needs radiology, and radiology can't be done at home.
This left users with two options, and neither was good:
Users who wanted home sample collection had to go to a centre and wait. That took time out of their day for something that should have been quick.

figures.alt: Full body checkup today equals inconvenient choices: two separate bookings or one combined package that forces a centre visit
One booking, complete checkup, your choice: pathology at home or centre, radiology at centre

content.quote: How might we let users book a complete checkup, pathology and radiology, in a single booking, while still letting them choose home or centre for pathology?

cards.label: Partners
cards.title: No single lab does both
cards.text: No lab partner offers both home pathology collection and centre-based radiology together.

cards.label: Physical
cards.title: Radiology needs a centre
cards.text: Radiology tests can't be performed at home. They need special machines.

cards.label: Scheduling
cards.title: No single time slot
cards.text: A combined package can't have one time slot for both pathology and radiology.

cards.label: Backend
cards.title: Two orders underneath
cards.text: Pathology and radiology come from different labs, so each runs as its own order with its own status.

content.label: 03 Root cause
content.heading: The barrier was the forced centre visit
paragraphs: It started with funnel data. My PM noticed that packages with radiology converted noticeably worse than pathology-only packages. I went through the data with my PM to confirm the pattern, and it held.
These checkups are employer-covered benefits, so users don't pay for them. Cost wasn't the reason. Something else was stopping users from booking radiology.

The system assumed every booking was either fully at home or fully at a centre. When a package had both pathology and radiology, it couldn't split them. So it picked the stricter option and sent users to a centre for everything.

figures.alt: The data showed a clear gap: pathology-only packages convert high, pathology plus radiology packages convert low
User at risk and business at risk: a fragmented journey hurts users and leaks revenue

content.quote: If we keep pathology at home, send users to a centre only for radiology, and put both in one booking, hybrid packages should complete at a rate closer to pathology-only packages.

content.label: 04 Borrowing a pattern
content.heading: Booking two labs like a round-trip flight
paragraphs: The biggest challenge was on the partner side. No single lab partner offered both home pathology and centre radiology. So the fix had to combine two partner labs into one booking.
There was no existing pattern in diagnostics to borrow. A stakeholder suggested looking at how travel apps like MakeMyTrip handle round trips, where two separate flights are booked in one checkout.
We used the same model: two lab partners instead of two flights, combined into one order and priced as a single combo.

figures.alt: A travel app showing outbound and return flights selected together
Flight fare options for a round trip, booked as one

content.label: 05 The solution
content.heading: The redesigned booking flow
paragraphs: The Lab Listing screen is the core of the redesign. No single lab could do everything, so the screen shows around fifteen partner combinations instead. Each one pairs a pathology lab with a radiology lab, sorted by distance and shown as a single card.

Users were being asked to trust two lab brands at once, and some of them were unfamiliar. So I added trust signals to the card itself: NABL and ISO accreditation badges on each partner logo, and instant-confirmation tags.
In the backend, each combo was two separate sub-orders under one parent order. If one partner needed to reschedule, the other half of the booking was not affected.

figures.alt: Before: packages with a single category, missed bundling opportunities and unclear lab information
After: intent-based search, capability-first filtering, a hybrid slot picker and single checkout
Select Lab Partners screen with Thyrocare and Apollo Diagnostics shown as one combo card
Design decisions on the Labs home page: offer tags, lab network indicator, trust badges, hybrid packages, family profiles
Lab listing screen decisions: partner combo cards, fulfilment tags, dual-address alignment, test type segregation, lab details

content.label: 06 Slots, review and status
content.heading: Two sets of steps in one booking
paragraphs: Slot selection, order review and order status follow the same idea. It is one order, with separate steps for pathology and radiology.

For slot selection, I reused the bottom sheet users already knew from single-package bookings. It has two tabs in order, pathology first, radiology second, and each one gets a tick when confirmed before the user moves on.
Order review and order status show both parts clearly, but always present them as a single booking.

figures.alt: Slot selection, order review and order status screens for a combined pathology and radiology booking

content.label: 07 Where it stands
content.heading: Live, with results still to come
paragraphs: This flow is live, but it is not fully validated yet. I expect that one order with two guided steps, instead of two separate checkouts, will reduce drop-off.
Once it has been live for a while, these three signals will show whether it worked:

figures.alt: Expected business impact: booking conversion, operational efficiency, package completion rates

cards.label: Signal 01
cards.title: Hybrid package adoption
cards.text: Are more users choosing packages that include radiology?

cards.label: Signal 02
cards.title: Fulfilment completion
cards.text: Do both halves of the booking actually get completed?

cards.label: Signal 03
cards.title: Less split-order drop-off
cards.text: Do fewer users stop after pathology and skip radiology?

content.heading: Thanks for reading about the hybrid package redesign
content.text: Building a healthcare super-app means solving a lot of logistics problems. This project was one of them.
